claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation is governed by a dynamic balance between passive-film formation and mechanical film removal.
The governing film is dense, self-healing, and enriched in oxidation-resistant elements.
Mechanical wear periodically removes the passive film during sliding.
Favorable oxidation kinetics allow the removed film to reform rapidly and maintain surface coverage.
Rapid film reformation limits exposure of bare metal to the electrolyte.
Limiting bare-metal exposure reduces corrosive dissolution by reducing active anodic sites.
The passive film reduces mechanical wear by acting as a lubricious barrier.
A sufficiently continuous film shifts degradation from direct metal-solution attack to a diffusion-limited process.
Microstructural homogeneity promotes continuous passive-film formation.
A conventionally processed baseline alloy has a discontinuous or less-adherent passive layer.
The baseline alloy consequently experiences greater mechanical wear and corrosion.
High-temperature sintering or annealing can promote surface enrichment of oxide-forming elements and formation of a dense, continuous passive film.
Silicide pack cementation is a feasible route for applying a surface coating to a high-entropy alloy.
The film-optimized alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than the matched baseline.
The film-optimized alloy will have shallower wear tracks than the matched baseline.
The film-optimized alloy will have lower total mass loss than the matched baseline.
The total degradation rate of the optimized alloy will be limited by the rate of film reformation between wear cycles.
The predicted protection should hold at moderate loads and temperatures that permit adequate film-reformation kinetics.
The protection should fail when mechanical stress exceeds the film's adhesion or reformation capacity.
At sufficiently high loads or temperatures, the film can break down faster than it heals.

contradictions.description: The governing mediator is repeatedly described as an in-situ-formed, self-healing passive oxide, but the intervention also permits a pre-applied silicide coating and the mediator calls a silicide-based film an example of an oxide film. A silicide coating is not itself an oxide and is not necessarily regenerated by the proposed oxidation-driven healing mechanism.
